en: Table of Contents for the *Brief Record of Miraculous Responses of the Avataṃsaka* The Twin Boys Manifest Auspicious Omens;
Heaven and Earth Present Signs of Good Fortune; Earthquakes and Radiant Light Manifest Spiritual Resonance;
Profound Enlightenment is Attained; the Sutra Shines with Five Colors; Divine Beings Provide Guarded Protection.
Celestial maidens attend upon him as winter chrysanthemums bloom in splendor; auspicious birds carry flowers and divine beings extend invitations.
Samantabhadra bestows the meaning of the teachings, and from his mouth emerge śarīras.
Bodhisattvas surge forth as the asuras retreat from the battlefield, and he realizes the entry into the unborn (*anutpāda*).
At that time, rain poured down; he was born within the Flower Treasury (Huāzàng) and received the Flower-Sound (Huáyīn) from a deity.
He was invited to lecture in a celestial palace, where the floodwaters were cut off and divine light repeatedly manifested.
Hell was extinguished, bathing water brought relief to the living, and auspicious clouds appeared as omens.
Brief Record of Miraculous Responses from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: A Monk of Different Lineage Receiving the Imperial Edict,
the Mountain Deity Listening to the Sūtra, the Golden City Radiating Splendor, and the Five-Colored Dragon Light.

Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhuhong of Yunqi Monastery in Ancient Hangzhou. The Manifestation of Auspiciousness by the Twin Boys: The Translation of the *Buddhabhadra-sūtra*. Originally, when the Buddha was translating the scriptures at Daochang Monastery, there were always two blue lotuses in the pond before the hall. Each time the Buddha recited a chapter of the scripture, one of the lotuses would bloom; once the recitation was finished, the lotus would wither and die. This occurred repeatedly. Later, when the monk Buddhabhadra arrived and began translating the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he saw the two blue lotuses blooming again as before. He then understood that these were auspicious signs from the Buddha’s past merit. He subsequently named the monastery "Lotus Flower" (Lianhua) after this event. It is said that the two boys were manifestations of the Buddha’s transformed body. The youth Yee emerged from the pond, holding fragrant flowers in his hands; the entire assembly beheld him.
Because this sutra had long resided in the Dragon Palace, the Dragon King, moved by a sense of joy and reverence, transmitted it for circulation and thus served as its attendant.
Heaven and earth presented auspicious omens for the Tang dynasty.
In the third month, on the fourteenth day of the first year of the Zhengsheng era—the Xinyou day—Śikṣānanda retranslated [the text].
On the preceding day, the Gengshen day, Empress Wu had dreamed that within the entirety of the heavens, sweet dew descended. One day later, on the Renxu day...
Furthermore, a sweet rain fell. When the new sutra was first translated, the Emperor issued an edict ordering Master Xuanzang to deliver a lecture on it.

On the twelfth day of the twelfth month, as the lecture reached the passage concerning the trembling of the Flower Treasury World-Ocean (*kusumatalagarbhavyūha-lokadhātusamudra*), the lecture hall and the monastery suddenly shook.
At that time, several thousand monastics and laypeople witnessed this together and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.

Regarding the "Earthquake Light-Stream" from the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions): it is said that when the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu was initially devoted to the Hīnayāna, his elder brother Asaṅga feigned illness to summon him.
Consequently, he opened the way for the Mahāyāna teachings, saying: "Before I pass away, read the sūtras that I have studied."

The Director [of the Library] immediately read the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and beheld the Dharma-realm of Vairocana and the ocean of Samantabhadra’s practices. Thereupon, he gave rise to faith and realization, exclaiming:
"I should take a sharp sword and sever my own tongue-root, to clarify the fault of my past praise of the Hīnayāna. His elder brother stopped him, saying:
"It is like a person who falls because of the ground and yet rises because of the ground. In the past, you used your tongue to disparage the Mahāyāna..."
"Ride upon it now; you may use your tongue to praise the Mahāyāna. He then entered the mountains to study the Mahāyāna scriptures and composed the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra*.
On the day the treatise was completed, the great earth shook everywhere and a brilliant light shone forth.

In the Taihe era of the Northern Qi dynasty, the third prince, moved by a profound spiritual resonance and awakening, sought Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva at Mount Qingliang. He performed the offering of self-immolation,
and his attendant, the palace official Liu Qianzhi, having witnessed this act of self-immolation, submitted a memorial requesting permission to enter the mountains.

He practiced the Way and subsequently took this sutra with him, diligently applying himself day and night through prostrations, repentance, recitation, and study, while praying in his heart for wondrous enlightenment.

For nearly twenty-one days, he abstained from grain and subsisted only on water; though his physical strength and breath were diminished, his sincere devotion grew ever more fervent. Suddenly, he was moved by a spiritual response such that his beard and mustache grew back completely.

Furthermore, there was the man Zhongxiang, whose spiritual brilliance was penetrating and enlightened, and who thoroughly understood the profound principles. He composed this scripture and its treatises, totaling six hundred fascicles.

Additionally, during the Later Wei dynasty, there was Lingbian, who had planted superior roots of goodness in past lives. Upon encountering the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he devoted himself with particular intensity to its study and veneration.
He then carried this sūtra upon his head and entered Mount Qingliang, seeking the secret protection of Mañjuśrī. After a full year had passed, his feet were covered in blood from the soles.
His flesh wasted away and his bones were exposed. Suddenly, he heard a voice from the air saying, "Cease [your toil]; simply contemplate this sutra.
Thereupon, he opened the scroll and attained sudden, great enlightenment. He then composed the *Huayan Yanyi Shiwen* (Exegesis on the Meaning of the Avatamsaka Sutra) in one hundred fascicles.
After the scripture was adorned with five-colored luster,
Yanming, Prince of Anfeng, and Yuanxi, Prince of Zhongshan, both of the Later Wei dynasty, set their minds upon the Unsurpassed [Vehicle] and prostrated themselves before the Perfect Doctrine.
They once mixed incense with ink to transcribe one hundred copies of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and one copy of the *Golden Letter Sūtra*, all in five [colors].

Incense served as the inner repository, and the seven treasures formed the outer casket. On a serene night at an auspicious hour, while he was practicing the Way in pure fasting, he immediately emitted a divine light;
its five colors were brilliantly radiant, illuminating the terrace and the halls.

The divine protector of the monastery was the monk De-yuan, who constantly took the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as his primary practice. He cultivated a pure garden, planting various grains and paper mulberry trees, as well as fragrant herbs interspersed with fresh flowers.
Whenever he entered the garden, he would invariably wash himself and put on clean robes before irrigating it with scented water.
The paper was produced from the *zhù* tree; after three years, its fragrance spread in all directions. Later, it was used to transcribe scriptures.

As soon as several lines had been written, each character emitted light that illuminated the entire courtyard. A divine being appeared, holding a halberd, manifesting his form to provide guard. There was also a blue-robed brahmin youth.
Holding celestial flowers in her hands, she suddenly offered them as an act of worship.
A heavenly maiden attended to the Elder Li of the Tang, whose name was Tongxuan. When he first arrived in Taiyuan, he stayed at the home of Gao Shanu; every morning he took only [vegetarian] food.
He took ten jujubes and one *bǎiyè* (cypress-leaf) cake, then set out on his way. On the road, he encountered a tiger that crouched submissively across the path as if waiting for him.
The Elder said to it, "I am about to compose a treatise to explain the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; you should find a place for me to dwell.
The tiger carried the Elder’s bag and bowl for over thirty li until they reached an earthen cave, where [the tiger] then...
He sat in a squatting posture. When the elder entered the grotto, there was originally no water within it. That evening, amidst wind and thunder, a great old pine tree was uprooted;

from beneath the tree, a spring emerged, its water clear, crisp, and sweet. While the elder was composing his treatise, two maidens of peerless beauty appeared, drawing water and burning incense to provide him with paper and brushes.
At the hour between the卯 and 辰 periods, they would invariably prepare pure meals, their comings and goings remaining unknown. Thus he completed his treatise.
Upon his death, he immediately vanished without a trace.

During winter, the *huángkuí* (Dongkui) flowers bloomed with vibrant beauty. Táng Dèng Yuǎnshuǎng was a native of Huáyīn. During the Zhèngshèng era, a relative of his died suddenly; seven days later, he revived and said:

In the afterlife, she intended to pursue her son, Shuang. Terrified, Shuang was advised by someone to copy the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Once the copying was finished, there was previously a Chinese aster (shǔkuí) growing beside his mother’s tomb;

though it had withered by winter, it suddenly burst into bloom, shining brilliantly and flourishing luxuriantly. The local community marveled at this, reported it to the court, and the family was honored as a "Gate of Filial Piety."

The monk Facheng, a practitioner of auspicious birds who carried flowers, lived in seclusion at Langu Valley. Later, he constructed a Huayan Hall on the Southern Ridge and depicted the images of the seven locations and nine assemblies.

He devoted himself to their veneration with single-minded diligence. Subsequently, an auspicious bird of extraordinary appearance and form appeared; it carried a flower into his room and circled around him.
He made offerings.
A divine being invited him to the Sui dynasty.
The monk Huiewu of the Chan Meditation Center was a native of Jingzhao. He once lived in seclusion with another monk on Mount Zhongnan. Huiewu...

Huayan received the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, while the other two maintained the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Each lived in seclusion, eating only wood-shavings and dwelling among the crags, each devoted solely to his own practice.

Suddenly, a man came to invite them to a meal at his residence. The two monks deferred to one another; the man said, "I invite Master Huayan. Zhiwu followed him accordingly, for he was actually a mountain deity.
He had invited a thousand arhats, all of whom deferred to the Venerable Zhiwu. Once the meal was finished and they had departed, the deity called for a youth.

The Master commanded him to serve as an attendant; he then entered the Master’s mouth and subsequently attained the state of an immortal (*ṛṣi*). He returned to retrieve the scriptures, took leave of his friends, and departed, treading upon the void with boundless ease.

Puxian Shouyi Sengbiancai was a person of unknown origin. In his youth, he served Dharma Master Yu and took the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* as his primary field of study. After a long time, however, he remained without realization.

He then separately maintained the rules of purity, fashioned an incense casket to hold the scriptures, and carried them upon his head while practicing the Way. This continued for three years, after which he dreamed—
Samantabhadra instructed him in the profound meaning [of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*], and suddenly he was able to recite it; it appeared as clearly as looking into a mirror.
Tang Fan Xuanzhi of Anding obtained śarīra in his mouth. At a young age, he took refuge with Master Dushun. Dushun ordered him to recite the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

He took this as his vocation and, relying on this very sutra, cultivated the practices of Samantabhadra. Every time he recited the scripture, he frequently obtained śarīras from within his mouth, numbering several hundred grains in total over the course of time.
The Bodhisattva’s Emergence from the Earth.
During the Tang dynasty, the monk Huiyou of Chongfu Monastery was diligent and austere in his observance of the precepts. He served Master Yan and specialized in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
At dawn and during the quiet hours of the night, he would burn incense and recite the "Emergence" chapter with sincere devotion. Suddenly, he saw more than ten bodhisattvas emerge from the earth.
They emerged, manifesting golden bodies that all radiated light; sitting upon lotus seats, they joined their palms and listened to the recitation.
When the sutra was finished, they vanished, and the asuras retreated from the battle array.
There was a śrāmaṇera from the kingdom of Khotan named Prajñāmiga-bhaṭa. He strictly maintained his observance of the precepts and specialized in reciting the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Suddenly, a person appeared before him with palms joined and said, "The devas invite you, Master. I pray that you close your eyes. In an instant, he arrived in the heavens.

The Lord of Devas knelt and entreated him, saying, "We are currently at war with the asuras and have repeatedly been defeated and routed. We beg you, Master, to recite the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* for us, hoping [that we may prevail]."

Through the empowerment of the Dharma, the Master ascended a celestial chariot and meditated upon the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. As he confronted the powerful enemy with the hosts of devas, the asuras suddenly broke and scattered.
He was escorted back in an instant, his body suffused with celestial fragrance that did not fade for the rest of his life.
The Master Wusheng Jietuo, whose secular surname was Xing, was a native of Wutai County in Daizhou. He entered the monastic order at the age of seven.

Initially, he followed Chan Master Huichao, who held him in high esteem for his potential. Later, at Mount Wutai, he specialized in the recitation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and practiced meditation according to the scripture, seeking a direct vision [of the Buddha].
Mañjuśrī manifested his body and instructed him, saying: "You need not pay homage to me now; you should instead reproach yourself. You will surely attain great awakening.
Because he sought it within himself, he awakened to non-arising (*anutpāda*). Moved by this, the Buddhas appeared and spoke this verse for him:
"The Dharma of the Buddhas is quiescent and profoundly deep; Only after practicing through vast eons is it now attained. If one can open and clarify this eye of Dharma,"
All Buddhas rejoiced in this. He asked about the Dharma of liberation and quiescence: "If it can be explained, may I be taught how to lead others?
The Buddhas then vanished, and a voice spoke again, saying: "Skillful means and wisdom serve as a lamp to illuminate the realm of the mind;
when one seeks the true Dharma within emptiness, there is nothing at all to be seen. Furthermore, while on the road he thought of burning incense, and in the air—
The voice said: "Joining the palms constitutes the flower; the body serves as the vessel of offering; the virtuous mind is the true incense;

and the fragrance of praise spreads like smoke. When the Buddhas smell this fragrance, they follow the sound to come and deliver us. All you people, exert yourselves with diligence; never again fall into doubt or error.
Thus it is called "Verses of Praise Arranging the Void."
At that time, there was the monk Daoying.
His surname was Chen, and he was a native of Puxian. At the age of eighteen, his parents arranged a marriage for him; they lived together as husband and wife for five years.
He vowed never to touch [women] again. Later, he studied the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* under Dharma Master Ju of Bing County and subsequently shaved his head.
He entered Baiti Monastery on Mount Taihang to practice *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. During a severe drought, he lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* to pray for timely rain.
There were two old men, each attended by two youths, who came at times to listen to the lectures. [The Master] found them extraordinary and questioned them; he then realized they were sea deities.
Consequently, he said, "Now, for the sake of the donor, please send down a fine rain. The old man commanded his two youths, and the youths immediately emerged from the window lattice.
In a short while, a great rain poured down in torrents, upon which those far and near all relied.

Huazang Shousheng (華藏受生) was a man of the Di (狄) people from Sui. With a spiritual and upright nature, he left the household life under Dharma Master Yan. At the age of eighteen, he was already able to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

He constantly relied upon the sutra to practice the contemplation of the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang guan*) as well as the contemplation of Maitreya’s Tuṣita Heaven. When his illness reached its terminal stage, his eyes gazed upward as if seeing something.
He saw this. When the monk Tongzhen questioned him, he replied: "I still see a youth in blue robes leading me to Tuṣita Heaven;

yet celestial bliss is not lasting, for one will ultimately fall back into the cycle of saṃsāra. The Lotus Treasury (Padmagarbha) is my true aspiration. Having said this, his breath ceased. After a short while, he revived again.
Tongzhen asked once more: "What do you see now? He replied: "I see great waters filling everywhere, with lotuses as large as chariot wheels."
And sat upon it. My wish was fulfilled. Shen Shouhua (Divyākāra) was from Song;
Guṇabhadra was a man from Central India. He opened the casket and took out the scriptures, immediately obtaining the *Avataṃsaka*. Later, Qiao...
The King invited him to lecture. Because he had not yet mastered the Chinese language, he performed ritual repentance and earnestly invoked Avalokiteśvara to pray for a divine response.

Consequently, he dreamed of a divine being who, holding a sword, took a person’s head and replaced it with another. Upon waking, his understanding of the Chinese language was suddenly and completely restored.
He then lectured on the Great Sūtra dozens of times.

During the Wei dynasty, Ratnamati, a native of Central India, was invited to the Heavenly Palace (the Imperial Court) to lecture. He was a man of vast learning and extensive scholarship who possessed profound insight into the principles of dhyāna.

Upon his initial arrival in Luoyang, he translated the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra*. The Emperor frequently ordered him to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and his refined interpretations were exceptionally brilliant. Once, while he was seated upon the high throne, suddenly—

There were those holding ceremonial tablets and carrying invitation cards, appearing like high-ranking officials, who announced: "The Celestial Emperor has come to invite the Dharma Master to lecture on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
The *dougao* and *weina* were also required to be present. The assembly of monks at the lecture hall all saw this simultaneously.
The Master smiled with serene joy and, bidding farewell to the multitude, passed away upon his Dharma seat; the *dougao* and others likewise entered *nirvāṇa* at the same moment.

During a flood that cut off the flow of a stream, Master Dushun—whose secular surname was Du and whose religious name was Fashun, and who was a native of Duling in Jingzhao—was engaged in his studies of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

He once lived in the mountains and intended to plant chrysanthemums; however, the ground was infested with many insects and ants. The Master then walked along the boundaries to demarcate the plot, whereupon all the insects moved outside.
He moved to San-yuan County. There was a man who had been deaf and mute since birth; the Master summoned him and spoke with him, and as soon as the man responded, he was healed.
Subsequently, the Master went to Nan-shan, where he encountered the flooding of the Heng-qu River. He halted the flow and crossed over it by walking slowly. On the day of his passing...
He universally gathered those with whom he had a karmic affinity; his voice and countenance never changed. When his speech ended, he passed away, and his spiritual responses were manifold.
According to a separate tradition, he was an emanation of Mañjuśrī, and divine radiance appeared repeatedly.
During the Tang dynasty, there was Fazang, whose courtesy name was Xuanshu. His mother conceived him after dreaming of a wondrous light.
Later, while the Dharma Master Yan was lecturing on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at Yunhua Temple, Fazang went to visit him. At midnight, he saw a divine radiance illuminating the courtyard and buildings;

the master sighed, saying, "A person of extraordinary character shall arise to propagate this vast and great teaching. When dawn broke, he encountered Master Yan, from whom he then devoted himself as a disciple.

He delved deeply into the inexhaustible. Later, while he was expounding the teachings at Yunhua Temple, a radiance issued from his mouth and in an instant formed a canopy, which was witnessed by the entire assembly.

The *Diyu Xiaomie Zuangling Ji* (Records of Miraculous Responses on the Annihilation of Hell) states: Wang Minggan, a native of Jingzhao, had never cultivated roots of goodness in his life. He fell gravely ill and died suddenly;
as he was about to enter hell, he saw a monk who taught him a verse, saying: "If a person wishes to fully understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, they should..."
One should contemplate in this manner: "The mind creates all Tathāgatas. One who recites this verse can dispel the various sufferings of hell.
After that person has recited it, they enter to see the King, who then releases them. At the moment the verse is recited, wherever the sound reaches, those suffering there all attain liberation.
This passage from the Jin dynasty scripture differs slightly from the last two lines of the current Tang dynasty scripture.
Guanshui Jisheng (盥水濟生) was the monk Śākyamitra, a native of Siṃhala. Having realized the third fruit [of the śrāvaka path], he arrived in China at the beginning of the Lín-dé era.

Emperor Gāozōng treated him with great reverence and respect. Later, he traveled to Mount Qingliáng to pay homage to Mañjuśrī and reached the West Taiyuán Monastery. At that time, it so happened that...
The monks were reciting the Avataṃsaka Sūtra. He asked, "What sūtra is this? They replied, "The Avataṃsaka.

His countenance changed with solemnity, and he said, "I did not know that this land also possesses such a sūtra. Joining his palms in praise, he remarked, "This Mahāvaipulya is of inconceivable merit."

According to tradition in the Western Regions, there are those who read this sutra and wash their hands with water; even those insects and ants moistened by that water which lose their lives will all be reborn in the heavens.

During the auspicious manifestation of the "Cloudy Landscape" (Jingyun) omen in the Tang dynasty, there appeared the National Teacher Qingliang, whose name was Chengguan and whose courtesy name was Daxiu. A native of Kuaiji, he belonged to the Xiahou clan.
He was born in the Wuyin year of the Kaiyuan era under Emperor Xuanzong. He stood nine chi and four cun tall; his hands reached below his knees when hanging down, and his mouth contained forty teeth.
His gaze would flash at night, yet during the day he did not blink. In the second year of the Jiànzhōng era of Emperor Dēngzōng, he began writing his commentary, first seeking an auspicious sign.
One night, he dreamed that a golden countenance stood as majestic as a mountain, its radiant features brilliantly clear.

Upon waking, he knew this was a portent of the "Universal Radiance" (Samantaprabhāsa). From then on, his pen never faltered; after four years, the text was completed. Furthermore, he dreamed that he transformed himself into...
The dragon raised its head toward the Southern Terrace and its tail toward the Northern Terrace, twisting and turning as it soared through the void.

In an instant, it manifested in hundreds and thousands of forms, winding through the azure heavens before dispersing in the four directions. Those who recognized it regarded this as a sign of the spreading of the Dharma.

When he first lectured for the assembly, auspicious clouds were moved to gather in the sky, swirling into the shape of a canopy. In addition to his commentaries and sub-commentaries, he further composed the *Shoujing* (Hand Mirror) in one hundred fascicles.

*Juan* (Scrolls), three fascicles; *Gangyao* (Essential Outlines), three fascicles; *Zhengyao* (Essential Points), one fascicle; *Xuanjing* (Mirror of the Profound), one fascicle; *Jingdeng Shuowen* (Explanatory Text on the Lamp of the Mirror), one fascicle; *Sansheng Yuanrong Guan* (Contemplation on the Perfect Fusion of the Three Sages), one fascicle;
and *Qichu Jiuhui Tuxin Shuowen* (Explanatory Text on the Diagram of the Mind from the Seven Locations and Nine Assemblies), one fascicle.

By imperial decree, the relevant authorities were ordered to cast an official seal for him, and he was promoted to the rank of State Preceptor (*Guoshi*) with the title Qingliang. On the sixth day of the third month of the third year of the Kaicheng era, he passed away at the age of ninety-nine.
In the morning, he served as the preceptor to seven emperors. He was one hundred and two years of age and had been a monk for eighty-three years.

His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on Mount Zhongnan. Not long after, a foreign monk arrived at the capital and submitted a memorial stating that he had seen two messengers passing through the sky atop Mount Xi;
he had halted them with a mantra and questioned them, to which they replied, "We are the deities of Mañjuśrī’s Hall in North India."
He traveled east to retrieve the Great Tooth of the Bodhisattva of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra and returned to his country to offer it worship. By imperial decree, he opened the stupa;
indeed, one tooth was missing, and only thirty-nine remained. He subsequently performed the cremation, during which the śarīra were radiant and lustrous, and the tongue was like a red lotus.
Consequently, the stupa was posthumously titled that of the National Teacher Qingliang.

Shan Shen Tingjing was from the Cao family of Chaocheng; his mother was of the Li clan of Lingqiu. His parents prayed at Mount Wutai before he was born. Once grown, he took his leave.
He visited Zhenrong Monastery on Mount Wutai and received the tonsure from Master Fashun.
He once recited the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in Liuniu Valley, subsisting only on grasses and trees. Whenever he recited the sutra, five or seven men dressed in Confucian robes would sit and listen;
they frequently brought rare flowers and fresh fruits as offerings. The Master questioned them in wonder, and they replied, "We are mountain deities. Having received the Dharma from you, Master..."

He possessed great power, yet he could find no way to repay [his teacher's kindness]. He wished to serve him as an attendant, but the Master did not take pleasure in it; consequently, he abandoned that place.

Jinguanghuiying (Golden City Radiant Reflection) was from Suvarṇaśrī in Central India; he was a monk of Nālandā Monastery who recited and maintained the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and was eighty years of age.
Fifth: She traveled by sea to pay homage at Mount Wutai. At each of the mountain peaks, she recited the ten volumes of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and practiced meditative stillness for seven days.
Within her state of concentration, she beheld golden walls, azure palaces, precious lotuses, fragrant waters, and shimmering nets of pearls, where celestial youths played.
Later, she passed away on Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*). Eight *he* of śarīra were obtained, as brilliant and lustrous as pearls.

He built a hut deep among the trees and devoted himself solely to reading the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, completing more than a thousand fascicles. Whenever he entered the contemplation of the Flower Treasury (*Huazang guan*), three...
On the fifth day he finally arose. The world then proclaimed that the Huayan Bodhisattva was about to manifest his passing into extinction.
His disciples requested a verse, and the Master said: "Throughout kalpas there has been neither going nor staying; in the application of function, what need is there for thought or deliberation?

Turning the body, one tramples through empty space; pay no heed to any right or wrong. Having spoken these words, he passed away. On that day, a dragon appeared upon his ritual altar, its five-colored radiance flying forth and illuminating [the surroundings].
